title: Vasudeva's Sacrifice
story:
The holy field of Samanta-panchaka lay open to the sky, a plain long consecrated by the rites of the wise, and that season the sages were doing something rare: they had chosen a man as their own. Vasudeva, Krishna's father, had come to them with a question about the highest duty, and the asking itself had pleased them. Now they took him as their disciple, and Vasudeva in turn chose them, as such rites direct, to be his priests, and they prepared to initiate him into a great sacrifice.

The field itself had its own gravity. For ages the wise had come to Samanta-panchaka to offer their rites, and the very ground was held to be blessed, so that a sacrifice performed there stood in a place already full of offerings. The sage Narada was among the gathered sages, watching the preparations take shape with quiet pleasure.

Word of the rite went out to every house of the Yadavas — Krishna's own people — and the clans came. From every direction the great families of the Vrishnis and the Yadavas converged on the plain, filling it with color and the low murmur of a whole people gathered for one purpose. When the initiation began, the Vrishnis arrived wearing lotus garlands, and Vasudeva's queens came with them, delighted, bright with gold and fine garments. The air filled with the sound of mridangas and drums, conches and kettledrums, until the whole field seemed to be singing. The priests anointed Vasudeva as the rite required, touched his body with fragrant unguents, and dressed him in silks and bracelets, necklaces, anklets and earrings, until the man who had come asking questions stood at the heart of the ceremony like a king at his crowning. His priests, too, were robed in jeweled silk, and the whole assembly shone under the open sky.

Among the kinsmen stood the two who made the gathering complete: Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, each surrounded by his own family and his own sons — sons among their father's people, the extraordinary standing quietly in an ordinary family gathering.

Vasudeva performed the rites as the tradition prescribed, the subsidiary offerings — the daily fire-offerings of agnihotra, and the rest — one after another, unhurried, with the great sages guiding every step. For days the fires burned, and the field breathed smoke and saffron and the scent of ghee, and the chant of the priests rose and fell with the sun. Then came the giving. At the proper time, as the scriptures direct, he gave the priests their dakshina, rich gifts of cows and land and maidens, so that the men who had conducted the sacrifice went away honored beyond anything they had asked. The queens made their offerings in turn, and the rite closed with the avabhritha bath, the final purification that brings a sacrifice to its end. When Vasudeva had bathed in that last water, he gave garments and ornaments to the bards and to the women who had graced the field; to his own kinsmen, with their wives and their sons, he gave abundant gifts, holding nothing back. Nor did he forget the wider circle: the assembled priests, the hosts of gods, men and ancestors, and the celestial singers called caranas, all were honored in their turn, so that no one who had taken part went away empty-handed.

When the drums had fallen silent and the fires had received their last oblations, Vasudeva stood on that holy field, cleansed by the bath and crowned with the dust of the rite. He looked across the plain at his sons, Krishna and Balarama, each at the head of his own house, and it seemed to him that the sacrifice had already given him everything a man could ask. The field of Samanta-panchaka had seen many great rites; it had rarely seen one so simply complete: a father purified, his sons beside him, and nothing held back from anyone who had come.
reflection: The account lingers not on the meaning of the rites but on the scene itself: the anointing, the music, the giving that leaves no one empty-handed. Its quiet center is the sight of Krishna and Balarama standing among their father's kinsmen, the extraordinary present in an ordinary family gathering.
next_story_tease: But in Dwaraka, a mother's grief was waiting, older than any sacrifice and not yet healed.
hero_scene: On the holy field of Samanta-panchaka, Vasudeva is anointed by his chosen priests amid mridangas, conches and kettledrums, while Krishna and Balarama stand among their kinsmen watching, the whole assembly shining under the open sky.
